title: Sahaj: effortless ease
hookLine: a natural, balanced calm that comes when striving settles

cards: Try to fall asleep. Really try. Squeeze your eyes, count harder, will yourself unconscious.
It doesn't work, does it? Or take a glass of muddy water. Stir it to clear it and it only gets cloudier.
Leave it on the table, and slowly the mud sinks and the water goes clear. Some good things can't be grabbed. They come when the grabbing stops.
The Gurus had a word for the calm that arrives that way: sahaj.

teach.b: Sahaj means natural, easy, what comes of itself.
The word is old: yogis and poets in India used it for a state beyond effort. In the Guru Granth Sahib it becomes one of the great words for a settled, balanced life.

You hear it in sahaj subhai, naturally, of its own accord, and in sahaj samadhi, a stillness that isn't a trance in a cave but calm in the middle of ordinary days. Sahaj isn't laziness, and it isn't giving up.
The Sikh way has plenty of effort in it: rising early, work, service, prayer. Sahaj is what happens to that effort when the ego stops gripping it.
Haumai, the self-centered I we met last week, is always straining: to be noticed, to win, to control. When it quiets, the same work goes on, only lighter.
The Anand Sahib, the song of bliss by Guru Amar Das, opens with anand, bliss, and sahaj arrives in the very next line.
In paraphrase: O my mother, bliss has come, for I have found the True Guru, and I found him with ease, sahaj. Not by conquering, not by some heroic feat. With ease.

teach.h: A HOME THE MIND COMES BACK TO.
teach.b: The hymns often picture sahaj as a home, the place the restless mind finally comes back to and sits down.
On an ordinary Tuesday, it might look like doing the dishes without fighting them. Listening without planning your reply. Working hard, and not being eaten by it.

how: Sahaj is a key word in Sikh scripture for natural, balanced poise; the Anand Sahib, which uses it in its first verse, is sung at many Sikh ceremonies and a short form is recited at the close of congregational services.

o: giving up all effort and simply doing nothing
a deep trance reached alone in a mountain cave
a natural ease that comes when the ego stops gripping

games.q: sahaj, turned four ways — tap the pairs.

s: sahaj means not trying at all
the Sikh way is full of work, service and prayer; sahaj is effort without the ego's grip.
the Anand Sahib speaks of finding the True Guru with sahaj
its first verse: bliss has come, the Guru found with ease.
in the Granth, sahaj samadhi means a trance far away in a cave
Sikh teaching ties it to stillness in the middle of ordinary life.

games.q: your mind is racing and you want calm right now. what does the picture of sahaj suggest?
o: force the calm by gripping harder.
stop stirring and let things settle, while you keep doing what's in front of you.
give up on everything for the day.
games.why: sahaj comes when the grabbing stops. like muddy water, the mind clears when it's left to settle, and the work goes on, lighter.

practice: Choose one small thing you can do right now, a sip of water, a stretch, folding your hands, and do it slowly, with no hurry and no performance, as if nothing is waiting. Notice the moment the effort stops pushing and just moves.
Then let the breath breathe itself, coming and going on its own, the way muddy water settles.

wordCard.voice: Sahaj. Natural, balanced ease; the calm that comes when striving settles, and the ego stops gripping the work.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sahaj, natural ease; the Anand Sahib uses it in its very first verse.

carryVoice: Your line: ease. The muddy water clears once you stop stirring it. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 917 (Anand Sahib, Ramkali Mahala 3, pauri 1)
